Article Title: A Virginia raccoon broke into a liquor store and passed out in 2025; a year later, merchandise inspired by its drunken escapade has raised more than $290,000 for an animal shelter
Article Text:
How a drunk raccoon became an unlikely face of a fundraiser

Fourteen bottles and a restroom floor

A raccoon that broke into a Virginia liquor store last year, sampled 14 bottles of alcohol and passed out in the bathroom has helped raise more than $290,000 for a local animal shelter through merchandise inspired by its drunken escapade.Nearly a year after the drunken escapade went viral, the Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter has raised thousands of dollars by selling merchandise inspired by the raccoon’s antics, The Washington Post reported.What are the odds of a raccoon that wrecked an Ashland, Virginia, liquor store last November becoming the face of a fundraiser for the Hanover County shelter? Apparently, not zero. The unlikely mascot has helped the shelter raise more than $290,000 through merchandise featuring its likeness and the slogan "Trashed Panda". It is the same shelter that took in the raccoon after it was found passed out in the store.“We never thought a raccoon would do this for us,” Jeffrey Parker, Hanover County’s chief of animal protection, told the outlet. The county did not come up with the merchandise idea on its own. Bonfire, a fundraising merchandise platform, reached out to the shelter after the story went viral. Animal protection officer Samantha Martin told the public-access Hear in Hanover podcast that the offer was simple: the company would make shirts and hand over the proceeds.“We didn’t think it was going to get this much money,” she said.The campaign’s goal was 19,500 items, and it has already sold 19,234. The campaign has raised $292,826. Bonfire’s catalogue now includes mugs, tumblers, stickers, shirts and hoodies bearing the nickname “Trashed Panda”.Ms Martin added that the shelter was desperately in need of funds, as it is “extremely old and the county is growing like wildfire”. The shelter can’t keep up. It needs more kennel space, a bigger well and a bigger shelter to accommodate the county’s growing population.Money from the sales is already being directed towards those needs. Hanover County officials approved body cameras for the department’s eight animal protection officers, and the devices are expected to be in use by January. The cameras are intended to record evidence for animal abuse investigations and complaints against officers.The break-in happened early on 29 November, according to WWBT. The raccoon came through the ceiling of the Virginia Alcoholic Beverage Control store and damaged the security system, triggering an alert from the monitoring company. The raccoon broke 14 bottles. By the time officers arrived, it was lying unconscious in the bathroom. An animal control officer took the “very intoxicated raccoon” to a shelter to recover.The raccoon spent several hours sobering up before being safely released back into the wild. The surveillance footage, which was later released, showed the raccoon moving through the Ashland, Virginia, ABC store after the break-in, including swaying among broken bottles and spilled alcohol.Soon, photos of the culprit’s drunken mishap were posted on the internet, and users did what they do best. They liked, shared and commented on the raccoon’s drunken escapade, and the story went viral. The incident even inspired asketch. The Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter realised that the viral raccoon could help them, and it did!Meanwhile, you can also purchase the “Trashed Panda” merchandise. The collection includes everything from T-shirts and sweatshirts to hats, mugs and stickers, with seasonal designs featuring slogans such as “Hot Trash Summer” and “Trick or Trashed”.
Article Summary: Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter has raised more than $290,000 through merchandise inspired by the raccoon's antics. The collection includes everything from T-shirts and sweatshirts to hats, mugs and stickers, with seasonal designs featuring slogans such as “Hot Trash Summer” and “Trick or Trashed” It is the same shelter that took in the raccoons after it was found passed out in the store.

Article Title: An Indiana worker died in a 2025 crash, leaving a widow, five children and a wrongful-death claim; after a battle over who would control his estate, a November 12 appeals court backed his daughter as
Article Text:
The court upheld the removal of Rebecca Johnson as co-administrator of Shane Fields' estate

Dispute over legal representation

Concerns over estate records and payroll

Appeals court rejects Johnson's challenge

An Indiana appeals court has upheld the removal of Rebecca Johnson as co-personal representative of Shane Fields' estate, leaving his daughter Hailey Daniels in charge. In its November 12 ruling, the court found that Johnson's refusal to follow court directions and cooperate with Daniels had affected the administration of the estate.According to the details of the case given in the judgement , Fields died in a road accident in Kentucky on January 31, 2025, while working for R&S Excavating. He was survived by his wife, Breanna, whom he married in 2023, and five children. His three adult daughters were Hailey Daniels, Paige Fields and Ryann Fields. His sons were Landon Patterson and Elijah Barnhart.The estate had few assets. Its main potential value came from a wrongful-death claim linked to the accident. The person appointed to represent the estate would therefore play an important role in pursuing the claim.Johnson, a family friend nominated by Breanna, sought appointment as personal representative in February 2025. Daniels opposed her request and filed a petition to take charge of the estate. In July, the trial court appointed both women as co-personal representatives. Their disagreement soon extended to the choice of lawyers for the wrongful-death case.Morgan and Morgan (M&M) filed a wrongful-death complaint in Kentucky on July 23, 2025, naming Johnson as the estate's representative and sole plaintiff. An amended complaint filed on August 5 added Breanna as an individual plaintiff.Daniels wanted the estate to hire local lawyer Robert Miles and his firm, Kolb Roellgen & Traylor LLP (KR&T). Johnson questioned Miles' experience and raised concerns about the firm's fees.KR&T proposed a fixed contingency fee of 33%. M&M initially proposed 30%, but its fee could increase at later stages of the case, including an appeal.The trial court asked the two representatives to agree on a law firm. When they failed to reach an agreement, it selected KR&T. Johnson challenged the decision and sought permission to appeal it, but the trial court rejected her requests.The court also raised concerns about Johnson making decisions without consulting Daniels. It directed her to explain why she should not face contempt proceedings or removal, noting that she appeared to have consulted Breanna instead of her co-representative.The disagreement also involved the handling of estate records. In September 2025, Johnson filed an inventory without discussing it with Daniels. Daniels told the court that it left out items including a gun safe, guns and an iPhone.Johnson had also obtained an employer identification number for the estate without consulting Daniels. She shared it only after the court issued an order seeking an explanation of her conduct.Another concern involved Fields' wages at R&S Excavating. The court proceedings showed that his wages had been issued in Breanna's name. It was alleged that this arrangement allowed Fields to continue receiving workers' compensation benefits from a previous employer while working at R&S.Johnson said she learnt about the arrangement after Fields' death, when a tax document showed income in Breanna's name. Daniels filed a police report. Johnson said she contacted R&S's workers' compensation insurer to ask about death benefits.The court also considered a possible conflict involving Johnson's husband, who worked at R&S and had been Fields' supervisor. Johnson acknowledged that legal action against the company could affect her husband's employment.Daniels sought Johnson's removal on December 9, 2025, citing the handling of estate records, the dispute over lawyers and her failure to follow court directions.At a January hearing, the trial court told Johnson that she had to sign KR&T's fee agreement or face removal. Johnson remained unwilling to sign unless Miles worked with more experienced lawyers.On March 4, the trial court removed Johnson and appointed Daniels as the sole personal representative. It approved KR&T's fee agreement, cancelled any agreement Johnson had entered into without Daniels' approval and directed Johnson to provide a final account and hand over the estate records.Johnson argued before the Indiana Court of Appeals that Breanna's nomination gave her priority under state law to represent the estate.The appeals court acknowledged that the surviving spouse's nominee had priority under the relevant law. However, it said this did not prevent a trial court from removing a personal representative found unsuitable.The judges found that Johnson had repeatedly refused to follow the trial court's directions on legal representation. They said she was required to comply with the orders unless they were overturned on appeal.The court also noted that the dispute had delayed the wrongful-death and workers' compensation claims. It said Johnson's conduct went beyond a disagreement between co-representatives and interfered with the administration of the estate.The concerns over the payroll arrangement, her husband's employment, the estate inventory and her dealings with M&M also supported the trial court's decision, the appeals court said.Johnson had further argued that the trial court should have selected M&M or allowed both firms to work together. The appeals court rejected this challenge, saying the trial court had the authority to choose counsel when the representatives could not agree.It found no reason to overturn the selection of KR&T. The firm had lawyers licensed in Kentucky, where the wrongful-death case was being pursued. The difference between the proposed fees was also not enough to show that the trial court had made an improper choice.Daniels will thus remain the sole personal representative of Fields' estate, with KR&T handling the wrongful-death claim.
Article Summary: An Indiana appeals court has upheld the removal of Rebecca Johnson as co- personal representative of Shane Fields' estate, leaving his daughter Hailey Daniels in charge. The court found that Johnson's refusal to follow court directions and cooperate with Daniels had affected the administration of the estate.

In Louisiana, a couple's 2016 divorce agreement required an ex-husband to pay his former wife's fuel and health insurance expenses; a court upheld the obligations after her remarriage and rejected her claim to half of a property sold for $500,000A Louisiana appeals court has upheld a 2016 agreement that a former couple made, ruling that an ex-husband’s contractual obligations to pay his former wife’s fuel and health insurance expenses did not automatically end when she remarried. The Third Circuit Court of Appeal issued its written opinion on October 30, 2026. It affirmed the trial court’s 2025 judgment in full. The same court rejected the woman’s claim to half the money from a house her ex-husband’s company later sold.The Louisiana couple married in 1994. The marriage lasted for 22 years, and they divorced in 2016. Following the divorce, the former couple signed a court-approved agreement that divided some of their property.Under that agreement, the woman could use of a 2014 Jeep and a 2015 Cadillac. She agreed to pay for their upkeep and insurance. Her ex-husband agreed to pay for her gas and to keep her on his health insurance. The gas promise went beyond those two cars. It covered “any other vehicles” she might use. A year after the divorce, the former couple signed a broader agreement. It said they would split equally any money from selling a house in Lake Charles.It said nothing about gas or health insurance.In Dec. 2017, a a quitclaim deed moved the house from a company owned by the woman to a company owned by her former husband. The woman’s attorney drafted the deed. It said the transfer was meant to carry out what the couple had agreed to. It did not say the sale money would be shared.In October 2022, the husband’s company sold the house to a third party for $500,000, according to the court’s opinion.After the sale, the woman went back to court, and asked the judge to cancel the deed and give her half the sale money. She also said that her former husband had stopped paying for her health insurance in March 2021. He stopped paying the gas payments in September 2022, three days after Amanda remarried. He then asked the court to stop his payments, saying her remarriage ended his obligation. A hearing officer agreed, recommending he pay $6,716.09 in past-due costs. In 2025, the trial judge ruled that the deed was valid. The judge also found that the payment terms were contract promises, not spousal support.Both sides appealed. The woman argued that the deed was a sham, but the and the appeals court disagreed. It said the deed’s words were clear, and judges may not read in between the lines. What’s written in the agreement matters, than what the parties meant. The court also said a sale is not a sham when something of value changes hands, even if no cash does. Here, the deal included avoiding a lawsuit and the benefits set out in the 2017 agreement. The woman’s claim that she still used the house also failed. The court said the record was thin. She used the property only with her ex husband’s permission, and she did not pay taxes or improvements.Now the question is about the gas charges and health insurance. Were those payments part of spousal support? This question matters, because state law usually ends support when the person receiving it remarries. However, in this case, the court observed, they were not. State support rules apply to support a judge's orders. These payments came from an agreement the couple made themselves. Their agreement does not mention an end date. The court said that did not change the result. Courts generally enforce deals that parties freely make, even if one side later regrets them.The appeals court found no clear error in the trial judge’s decision and refused to end the ex husband’s payments. As the payments were contractual obligations, not spousal support, the court did not consider his separate argument about remarriage. Both sides will share the appeal costs equally. Either party may also ask the court to rehear the case within the time allowed by Louisiana law.
Article Summary: A couple's 2016 divorce agreement required an ex-husband to pay his former wife's fuel and health insurance expenses. A court upheld the obligations after her remarriage and rejected her claim to half of a property sold for $500,000.

Article Title: A New York fraudster used forged deeds to steal two Harlem homes worth $4.7 million, leaving an elderly owner in a homeless shelter; after 14 years, a court sentenced him to up to 21 years in prison
Article Text:
Joseph Makhani gets up to 21 years for stealing two Harlem homes.

How Makhani took control of the first Harlem home

Second property involved a tenant's signature

Court orders prison sentence and restitution

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A New York man who used forged property documents to take control of two Harlem brownstones worth around $4.7 million was sentenced to up to 21 years in prison on Tuesday. Joseph Makhani's actions left an elderly homeowner without a home for years, while he collected rent from apartments in the stolen property.The ruling issued by Office of the New York State Attorney General Letitia James, found him guilty of stealing the two properties and carrying out a scheme to defraud. The case involved brownstones at 107 West 118th Street and 135 West 131st Street in Harlem.According to the sentence, Makhani had spent years deceiving people. His actions had caused problems for tenants and left the rightful owner of one of the properties homeless. “After years of scheming and deceiving New Yorkers, Joseph Makhani is finally facing justice,” James said.The case began in 2012, when Makhani started using fraudulent deeds, false documents and companies under his control to claim ownership of the two properties. The investigation later found that he had used different methods to take control of each building.A seven-week trial concluded in July this year, when a jury found Makhani guilty on three counts.These included two counts of criminal possession of stolen property in the first degree and one count of scheme to defraud in the first degree.One of the properties was located at 107 West 118th Street. The evidence presented during the trial showed that Makhani began using fraudulent documents to take control of the brownstone in 2012.A corporation controlled by Makhani claimed in a property filing that it had paid just $10 for the building. He later submitted a mortgage application in which he falsely stated that he had purchased the property for $975,000.The application helped him obtain a $650,000 construction loan for renovation work. He later refinanced the property and received a long-term mortgage loan worth $1.2 million.Makhani also submitted a forged application to the New York Department of Housing Preservation and Development. The application sought to convert the building into market-rate rental apartments.Between 2016 and 2023, he rented out the apartments in the building. Each unit was rented for as much as $3,400 per month, allowing him to collect more than $12,000 in monthly rent.The elderly homeowner, however, did not receive any money from Makhani. Despite being the rightful owner of the property, the person was forced to live in a homeless shelter for years. The brownstone was valued at approximately $2.9 million in 2023.Makhani also took control of another brownstone at 135 West 131st Street in Harlem. The evidence presented during the trial showed that he began using fraudulent deeds and other false documents to claim the property in 2012.The last genuine deed recorded for the building dated back to 1975. It was registered in the name of an elderly homeowner who died soon afterwards.Around 2012, Makhani approached one of the building's tenants and claimed that he had purchased the brownstone. He obtained the tenant's signature by pretending to offer him a job.Makhani then filed a fraudulent deed that falsely presented the tenant as the building's owner. This allowed him to transfer the property to a company under his control.In 2013, he attempted to evict the tenants and filed a lawsuit against them on behalf of his company. However, questions were raised about his ownership claim and the deed during the eviction proceedings.Makhani then filed another fraudulent deed. This document claimed that the heirs of the last recorded owner had transferred the property to his company. The brownstone was valued at approximately $1.8 million in 2018.The trial evidence also showed that Makhani arranged fraudulent civil lawsuits as part of his efforts to take control of both properties.Following the seven-week trial, the jury found Makhani guilty in July 2026. He was convicted of two counts of criminal possession of stolen property in the first degree and one count of scheme to defraud in the first degree.New York State Supreme Court Judge Michele Rodney sentenced him to four to 12 years in prison for stealing the property at 107 West 118th Street. He received another three to nine years for the theft involving 135 West 131st Street. These sentences will run consecutively.He was also sentenced to one and one-third to four years for the scheme to defraud. This sentence will run concurrently with the others. The combined sentence is seven to 21 years in prison.Makhani has also been ordered to pay $500,000 in restitution to Flushing Bank by May 7, 2027. The court will hold another hearing to decide whether the deeds and mortgage recorded against the property at 107 West 118th Street should be cancelled.
Article Summary: Joseph Makhani used forged documents to take control of two Harlem brownstones worth around $4.7 million. His actions left an elderly homeowner without a home for years, while he collected rent from apartments in the stolen property. A seven-week trial concluded in July this year, when a jury found him guilty on three counts.

Article Title: Outlander star Sam Heughan went back to the Scottish drama school where he trained to fund three scholarships every year; his separate creative award selected new student winners again in 2026, includ
Article Text:
From student to supporter

A separate platform for student creativity

Meet the 2026 winners

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Actor Sam Heughan is using the success he found through acting to help the next generation of performers get their start. The Outlander star, who trained at the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland (RCS) in Glasgow, has committed to funding three annual scholarships for students pursuing undergraduate studies at the institution. He has also created a separate initiative that gives emerging artists financial support to develop their own creative projects. According to the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland and its May 2026 announcement, Heughan's contribution extends beyond tuition assistance. Through his scholarship programme and the Write Start creative commission, he is helping students gain access to opportunities, mentorship and resources that can make it easier to take their first steps into the performing arts industry.Heughan's connection with the institution is a personal one. Born in Balmaclellan, Dumfries and Galloway, the actor graduated from RCS with a BA in Acting in 2003. He went on to build an international career, becoming widely recognised for playing Jamie Fraser in the historical fantasy series Outlander, based on Diana Gabaldon's novels.In July 2021, he announced his ten-year scholarship commitment, returning to the institution to help students who might otherwise struggle to afford studying in Glasgow.The programme provides three scholarships each academic year. Two are intended for Scottish students entering the BA Acting course, while the third supports a student from outside Scotland studying within the School of Stage and Screen. The financial assistance is intended to make professional arts education more accessible, particularly for students who face financial barriers to pursuing their ambitions. His contribution was also recognised by the conservatoire in 2022, when he received an honorary doctorate and returned to attend its graduation ceremony.Alongside the scholarships, Heughan established Write Start: The Sam Heughan Creative Commission in 2021. Unlike the scholarship programme, which helps students with their education, this annual initiative focuses on helping them turn original ideas into finished creative projects.The competition encourages collaboration between students from different disciplines, including music, acting, dance, filmmaking and production. It provides funding and professional guidance, giving students the opportunity to experiment with ideas that might otherwise remain on paper. The 2026 edition recognised projects that brought together different artistic approaches, with two main winners receiving £2,500 each and runners-up receiving £500.Among this year's recipients was music student Bohdan Ilnytskyi, who won the School of Music category for his project Some of Us. The £2,500 grant will support his exploration of how music can drive storytelling in films, rather than simply accompany scenes. His work also looks at incorporating Ukrainian musical instruments, including the kobza, into contemporary screen compositions. The School of Music runner-up award went to Isla Hallewell and her six-member ensemble, Mother Tongues: Ancient Folk. Their project will explore the relationship between historical Baroque music and folk traditions through a collaborative programme involving the University of Oxford and the Bates Instrument Collection.In the School of Stage and Screen category, second-year acting student Robert (Robbie) Greenhalgh received the other £2,500 award. His project, Swim Until You Can't See Land, will be developed with fellow students Shay McFadden and Morven Blackadder. The proposed theatre production or feature film draws inspiration from Scottish band Frightened Rabbit and its late frontman Scott Hutchison.The story follows a young man returning to his seaside hometown on Scotland's east coast after his brother's death, exploring grief, identity and the complicated relationship people have with the places they come from. The £500 runner-up award in the same category went to acting students Wren Callender, Kit Allen and Marcela Weltsek-Medina.Their project, The Boy and the Rat Bastard, is a queer satirical animated television concept for which they plan to develop a teaser trailer. The next edition of Write Start is expected to open for applications in 2027, with details due towards the end of the year.Through these two initiatives, Heughan has created different avenues for students to pursue their ambitions, whether by making formal training more affordable or giving original ideas the financial backing needed to take shape. For someone who once walked the same corridors as these aspiring performers, the effort is also a way of helping ensure that financial circumstances do not determine who gets the opportunity to build a career in the arts.
Article Summary: Heughan trained at the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland (RCS) in Glasgow. He has committed to funding three annual scholarships for students. The actor has also created a separate initiative that gives emerging artists financial support to develop their own creative projects. Heughan's contribution extends beyond tuition assistance.

NEW DELHI: Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second company employee, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters, after his resignation on Thursday.The latest revelation follows reports of two other extramarital relationships involving Huang, including one with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care.Reuters said it was not identifying the second employee. The controversy has raised questions about potential security risks involving the world's leading artificial intelligence chipmaker.

Article Title: US Senator Chris Van Hollen announces bid to replace Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader
Article Text:
Chuck Schumer (left) faces first leadership challenge in decades as Van Hollen enters race

Van Hollen gets support from Sanders, El-Sayed

Disagreement over Schumer's leadership

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the Senate Democrats consider a change in leadership after their recent electoral success? Yes, fresh leadership can bring new ideas. No, experienced leadership should continue. It depends on the party's future goals. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced a bid to become the next Senate Majority Leader, challenging incumbent Democratic leader Chuck Schumer after the party's victories in the US midterm elections.Van Hollen said on Thursday that he was running because “the American people called for change” and argued that Democrats needed new leadership to respond to the election result.“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”The leadership election will be held by secret ballot in early December. It is expected to be the first contested election for the position of Democratic leader in decades, with senators privately debating whether Schumer should continue in the role.Schumer has said he has enough support to retain the position. In a statement following Van Hollen’s announcement, he welcomed discussions about the future of the caucus and reiterated that he had the votes to remain its leader.“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”Schumer has been speaking to Democratic senators since the election and working on the party's agenda for 2027. During private caucus meetings this week, he outlined a broad plan for the first 100 days of the new majority.“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told the news agency Associated Press in an interview last week.Van Hollen has received endorsements from independent Senator Bernie Sanders , who caucuses with Democrats, and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.Sanders said the election result reflected a demand for a Democratic Party that would challenge powerful special interests and the billionaire class while fighting for working families.“The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats,” Sanders said.El-Sayed had also backed Van Hollen's leadership bid, saying the party needed “bold leadership” after the election.“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote on X. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”Sanders and Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan had called for new leadership at a press conference on Tuesday, although neither had then endorsed a specific candidate, AP reported.Several Democratic senators have publicly backed Schumer, including incoming Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted in last week's election.Maine Senator Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election, also defended Schumer after Van Hollen's announcement.“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” King said, adding that Schumer was “one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history”.The contest follows divisions within the Democratic caucus that became more visible in spring 2025, when Schumer faced criticism after siding with Republicans on a spending vote.Although he subsequently led Democrats through a government shutdown and helped the party's candidates during the midterm campaign, sections of the party's base have continued to call for generational change.Van Hollen, 67, is 75-year-old Schumer's challenger. He has presented himself as a new face for the party and has also said he is considering a presidential run.Speaking to MS NOW, Van Hollen said his decision to contest the leadership position was driven by what he described as a broader demand for change in Washington.“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people. We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day — red states, blue states, purple states — and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, led by a corrupt political system,” he said.Van Hollen also criticised Schumer's involvement in Democratic primaries, accusing him of supporting establishment candidates instead of focusing on defeating Republicans.“We shouldn't have a leader who is getting involved in picking sides in open Democratic primaries, and we should be focused on defeating Republicans. We have two senators right now in the Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way.He supported establishment candidates in the primaries,” he told MS NOW.Van Hollen has also called for action against President Donald Trump over allegations of corruption, supported efforts to impeach defence secretary Pete Hegseth and urged Congress to defund the war in Iran.The December ballot will determine who leads the Senate Democratic caucus as it prepares to take control of the chamber in the next Congress.
Article Summary: Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced a bid to become the next Senate Majority Leader. It is expected to be the first contested election for the position of Democratic leader in decades, with senators privately debating whether Schumer should continue in the role. Schumer has said he has enough support to retain the position.

Article Title: Spain Protest: Protesters clash with police, set fires during Spain's general strike: Watch
Article Text:
Protesters set fires, clash with police during Spain's general strike: Watch

Clashes broke out between masked protesters and police in Barcelona on Wednesday as tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike in 14 years, called by the country's major trade unions over the housing affordability crisis and rising cost of living.Around 120,000 people joined demonstrations in Madrid and more than 50,000 gathered in Barcelona, where some protesters set fire to rubbish bins, smashed shop windows and clashed with police. Officers fired tear gas to disperse the crowds, while transport and other public services across the country faced significant disruption.The disturbances in Barcelona continued into the evening, with a heavy police presence in the city centre. Some clashes took place along Passeig de Gràcia, near the iconic Plaça de Catalunya. Local media reported that protesters fired fireworks at police and looted shops, including a Lego store. Some were also seen attempting to enter an Apple Store.The unions said around four million workers participated in the nationwide strike, which was backed by Spain's two largest labour organisations, the UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants' associations protesting against rising rents and evictions.UGT chief Pepe Álvarez described the strike as a success, citing "massive" participation, while CCOO leader Unai Sordo said turnout was "very significant". However, participation varied across the country, with stronger support in coastal regions where housing pressures have been particularly acute.The walkout was the first general strike in Spain since 2012, when workers protested against austerity measures during the eurozone debt crisis. It comes less than three weeks before parliamentary elections scheduled for November 29.Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is seeking to make housing affordability a central election issue and shift the political debate away from corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. His Socialist Party, however, continues to trail in opinion polls.Spain faces a housing deficit of around 750,000 homes, which is projected to exceed one million by 2028, according to the country's central bank.With home ownership becoming increasingly unaffordable, demand for rental accommodation has risen sharply, putting further pressure on the market. The average monthly rent of 1,176 euros ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7 per cent of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
Article Summary: Around 120,000 people joined demonstrations in Madrid and more than 50,000 gathered in Barcelona. Some protesters set fire to rubbish bins, smashed shop windows and clashed with police. Officers fired tear gas to disperse the crowds, while transport and other public services across the country faced significant disruption.

Article Title: 'I may be jailed, they may try to kill me': Sheikh Hasina's defiant message on returning to Bangladesh
Article Text:
Hasina opens up on fears, threats and Bangladesh return

Denies ordering killings during 2024 uprising

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Rejects International Crimes Tribunal verdict

Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has said that the threat of arrest, imprisonment or even death would not stop her from returning to Dhaka, asserting that she would rather die in her homeland than stay away from her people.In a rare audio interview with news agency IANS, Hasina said she was fully aware of the risks involved in returning to Bangladesh but maintained that fear had never stopped her from doing what she believed was right.“Look, I understand the risks very well. I may be arrested the moment I arrive. They may send me to prison. They may even try to kill me. I have considered all these possibilities. But, you know, I stopped worrying about my personal safety a long time ago. I returned to Bangladesh in 1981, despite military rule. I returned again in 2007, knowing that the military-backed government might arrest me. I have faced imprisonment and repeated attempts on my life. Fear has never stopped me from doing what I believe is right,” the exiled leader stated.Expressing concern over the situation in Bangladesh, Hasina said the country was going through a difficult phase, alleging that Awami League leaders and workers were being persecuted while ordinary people were suffering and losing their homes and livelihoods.She said the hardships faced by the people had strengthened her determination to return and stand by them, irrespective of the consequences.“Today, my country is going through a terrible time. Our leaders and workers are being persecuted. Ordinary people are suffering, and families are losing their homes and livelihoods. How can I stay away while my people face such hardship? I have spent my entire political life with the people of Bangladesh. Whatever happens to me, I want to stand beside them. If I have to die, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina told IANS.Addressing allegations over deaths during the 2024 uprising in Bangladesh, the former prime minister categorically denied ordering the killing of innocent people.Hasina accused the former Muhammad Yunus-led interim government of stopping a judicial inquiry she had initiated into the deaths and subsequently granting legal protection to participants in the uprising for acts classified as “political resistance”.“Let me make one thing very clear. I never ordered the killing of innocent people. I reject that accusation completely. Every death was tragic. As Prime Minister, I had a responsibility to protect the lives of our citizens, and I wanted to know exactly what had happened. That is why, on July 18, 2024, I established a Judicial Enquiry Commission headed by a High Court judge. On August 1, I expanded it to a three-member commission so that every incident could be examined properly. But what happened after Muhammad Yunus assumed power? He stopped that investigation,” the former PM said.She questioned the interim administration's decision to halt the inquiry while pursuing murder cases against her and thousands of Awami League leaders, activists and workers.“His administration subsequently granted legal protection to participants in the uprising for acts classified as political resistance. At the same time, murder cases were brought against me and thousands of Awami League leaders, activists and workers. If they really wanted the truth, why did they stop the judicial investigation that I had already established? Why should there be different standards of justice depending on someone's political identity?” she questioned.Hasina also rejected the proceedings of Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) and the verdict against her, alleging that she was not given a genuine opportunity to defend herself.“As for the tribunal, I reject both the proceedings and the verdict. I was denied what I consider a genuine opportunity to defend myself. I will examine whatever lawful options are available to challenge that verdict,” she told IANS.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina says she would rather die in her homeland than stay away from her people. Denies ordering killings during 2024 uprising in Bangladesh. Rejects International Crimes Tribunal verdict against her. Says she was not given a genuine opportunity to defend herself.

Article Title: An 80-year-old New York heiress says her brother and daughters cut off $125,000 in monthly trust payments and pushed for a $2.5 million family investment; relatives deny wrongdoing and cite $23.5 mill
Article Text:
Constance “Connie” Milstein Photo credit: Dogtag.org

What Connie alleges

The family’s response

Representative imafe from Canva

The $23.5 million question

A family business with old wounds

What happens next

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A bitter legal dispute inside one of New York’s best-known real estate dynasties has returned to court, with 80-year-old Constance “Connie” Milstein accusing her brother and two daughters of cutting off monthly trust payments of $125,000 and seeking to pull $2.5 million from a trust tied to her name. The allegations, reported by the New York Post and Hoodline, have been strongly rejected by her relatives, who say the trust was created principally for her children and point to roughly $23.5 million in spending by Connie in recent years.The case is not simply a quarrel over money. It concerns who controls a family trust, how much discretion trustees may exercise, and whether a wealthy woman who once served as the United States ambassador to Malta can be treated as financially independent despite relying on regular distributions. Connie’s lawyers frame the move as pressure during settlement talks, while the other side says she is a discretionary beneficiary with substantial assets of her own. Read more details, as per the reports, here:Connie Milstein, granddaughter of the late Milstein patriarch Morris Milstein, filed the action in New York County Supreme Court against her brother, Philip L. Milstein, and her daughters, Abigail Black Elbaum and Joanna M.Milstein. Her petition alleges that, in the summer of 2025, trustees Peter Grossman and James Sligar told her they would stop the regular monthly distributions of $125,000 from a trust connected to her late mother, Vivian Milstein.Her lawyers argue that the trustees and family members knew Connie depended on those payments to meet her expenses. They describe the halt as a pressure tactic intended to force her back into settlement discussions with Philip and her daughters over long-running disagreements involving interests in the family’s businesses.The filing also alleges that Philip issued a drawdown notice requiring Connie’s trust to contribute $2.5 million to the family business by September 2025. Connie’s legal team says that demand, coming around the same time as the suspension of monthly payments, was another attempt to gain leverage in the negotiations.Connie is asking the court to replace Grossman and Sligar as trustees. Her lawyers allege that the two men worked with Philip and her daughters against her, accusations that the trustees and the family strongly deny.Relatives and the trustees have pushed back forcefully. In a counter-filing seeking dismissal of the lawsuit, they argue that the trust was created “for the express primary benefit” of Connie’s two children, rather than as a guaranteed source of support for Connie herself, as per the reports.Their legal memorandum says Abigail and Joanna, as primary beneficiaries, had the authority to remove and replace trustees, while Connie was only a discretionary beneficiary of that particular trust. The filing also says Connie has other trusts and can readily access assets, undermining the claim that she was left without financial options.A spokesperson for Philip and his family said the dispute was regrettable but described Connie’s petition as filled with “hyperbole and innuendo” and lacking legal or factual merit. The spokesperson did not explain why the daughters sought to stop the payments, according to the New York Post.Lawyers for Grossman and Sligar dismissed Connie’s allegations that they exploited her lack of liquidity as “a diversion not based in reality.” They also criticised what they called her “profligate spending habits,” setting up a sharply different account of her financial position.The defence claims Connie spent approximately $23.5 million over the past few years. According to the memorandum cited by the New York Post, that figure includes $7 million for a Montreal residence, more than $8 million for two homes in New Hampshire, over $5 million for jewellery and other personal items, and $3 million for an annual private aviation contract.The trustees’ lawyers also say Connie recently auctioned jewellery for $7.5 million, arguing that she had assets available to liquidate if necessary. Those figures are allegations made in court filings, not established findings, and Connie’s attorneys have called the counterfiling a “pathetic attempt at distraction.”The dispute therefore turns on a familiar but difficult question: can someone with substantial wealth still be financially vulnerable if most of that wealth is tied up in property, businesses, trusts or illiquid investments? Connie’s side says the monthly payments were essential to her lifestyle and expenses. Her relatives’ side says she is far from cash poor and has the means to support herself.The Milstein name carries enormous weight in New York real estate. Morris Milstein founded the Circle Floor Company, and his sons Seymour and Paul transformed it into a major property empire, developing apartments, hotels and office space while acquiring Emigrant Bank in the 1980s.The family’s holdings have included One Lincoln Plaza in Manhattan and the historic Jefferson Hotel in Washington, D.C. Forbes estimates the family’s assets at about $3.1 billion, and the Milsteins have also left a visible philanthropic mark through institutions including the American Museum of Natural History, NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital and the Metropolitan Opera.But the wealth has long been accompanied by conflict. Seymour and Paul reportedly clashed over succession, with Paul favouring his son Howard and Seymour favouring a division of the business. Their dispute produced lawsuits and a settlement in 2003, after Seymour’s death in 2001.The current fight involves the next generation. Philip co-founded Ogden Cap Properties with Connie and her daughter Abigail, while Grossman has represented the principals of Ogden and the Seymour Milstein family since 2002. Those overlapping business and legal relationships help explain why a disagreement over trust payments has become so personal and so difficult to resolve.For now, the court will have to decide whether Connie’s claims justify replacing the trustees, and whether the family’s arguments about the trust’s purpose and her spending are enough to defeat her petition. Neither side appears close to agreement, and the language in the filings suggests that the relationship between Connie, her brother and her daughters has deteriorated well beyond an ordinary financial disagreement.The case is also a reminder that inheritance does not always bring certainty. Even in families with billion-dollar portfolios, famous buildings and generations of business success, disputes over control, liquidity and trust authority can turn siblings and parents and children into adversaries. The Milstein litigation may ultimately settle privately, but until then it offers a rare public look at how one of New York’s most prominent real estate families is handling a conflict from within.
Article Summary: Connie Milstein, 80, accuses her brother and two daughters of cutting off trust payments of $125,000 and seeking to pull $2.5 million from a trust tied to her name. The allegations, reported by the New York Post and Hoodline, have been strongly rejected by her relatives, who say the trust was created principally for her children.

Article Title: A Massachusetts woman started growing mushrooms in her basement closet as a hobby; seven years later, her farm was producing around 1,000 pounds every week
Article Text:
Image Credit: AI generated

How a basement closet mushroom experiment became a growing farm

What made mushroom growing suitable for a small space

Demand pushed the operation beyond its original space

A larger facility transformed the small mushroom business

What mushrooms did the farm grow and sell

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The challenges behind expanding mushroom production

A mushroom-growing experiment that began in a basement closet eventually developed into a commercial farming operation producing hundreds of pounds of mushrooms every week. Julia Coffey, founder of Mycoterra Farm in Massachusetts, began cultivating mushrooms in January 2010, initially treating it as a small hobby business. What started with limited space and modest production gradually expanded as customers showed interest in her harvests. According to an interview published by Boston Voyager, Coffey reinvested earnings into the operation, eventually moving beyond her basement to greenhouses and, later, a dedicated farming facility.Coffey's journey into mushroom cultivation was shaped by earlier experience. In her interview with Boston Voyager, she explained that she had spent 4 years working at mushroom farmer Paul Stamets' farm in Washington state before returning to her hometown of Westhampton, Massachusetts, in 2009.After struggling to find fulfilling employment, she decided to start growing mushrooms in January 2010. The initial operation occupied a closet in her basement, with cultivation primarily intended as a hobby business rather than a large agricultural enterprise.The mushrooms soon found customers at local food co-operatives and farmers markets. Their reception encouraged Coffey to reinvest the money she earned, alongside income from other jobs, into expanding the farm.The early growth was gradual because mushroom-growing equipment was expensive. Rather than immediately investing in a large facility, she increased production as resources became available, allowing the business to develop at a manageable pace.Boston Voyager reported that Coffey purchased the house she was renting in December 2012, enabling her to expand the mushroom laboratory further into the basement. She also began growing mushrooms in the garage, although she later acknowledged that it had not been the best decision.The Fungi Academy explains why cultivation can be accessible to people without conventional farmland. A basement, garage, shed or spare bedroom can provide space for a small growing operation, while even a modest setup can produce mushrooms for household consumption.A basic mushroom-growing kit costing approximately $20 can provide two or three harvests with regular misting over around two weeks. A larger investment of roughly $100 beyond the kit could help someone establish a small urban mushroom farm capable of producing hundreds of pounds of gourmet and medicinal mushrooms.The approach does not mean that commercial farming is effortless. Coffey's experience illustrated how a small operation could become more demanding as production increased. Her initial success required her to invest not only in additional equipment but also in more suitable growing environments.As Mycoterra Farm attracted more customers, its original growing arrangements became increasingly difficult to maintain. Boston Voyager reported that Coffey's partner, Chris, joined the business in autumn 2013, bringing additional enthusiasm and helping her pursue further expansion.The first major expansion was completed in January 2015. The farm added an insulated container that served as a walk-in cooler, alongside two greenhouses measuring 24 by 48 feet. Insulation and radiant heating helped the greenhouses support mushroom production throughout the year.The additional space allowed Coffey to increase output, but it did not take long for the expanded operation to encounter another limitation. As production grew to fill the greenhouses, the farm was again approaching its capacity.Coffey hired three employees during 2015, while a family member who had previously helped at farmers markets also began working on the farm. The growing team enabled Mycoterra to handle a larger operation and its increasing customer demand.According to Boston Voyager, the farm eventually used pallet racks extending from the floor towards the ceiling to make the most of its greenhouse space. This arrangement helped increase production to approximately 500 pounds of mushrooms a week, although demand continued to exceed what the facility could supply.The next significant change came when Coffey and her partner discovered a vacant building that had previously operated as an equestrian centre. Boston Voyager reported that they encountered the property while making a delivery to a local restaurant around New Year.The building offered the space required to expand beyond the greenhouses. After months of negotiations and financing challenges, Coffey purchased the property in August 2016. But converting it into a mushroom-growing facility required extensive renovation.The farm finally moved from Westhampton to South Deerfield in December 2017. Boston Voyager reported that production quickly doubled to around 1,000 pounds a week following the relocation.Mycoterra Farm developed a range of specialty mushrooms. In her Boston Voyager interview, Coffey listed shiitake, lion's mane, chestnut, nameko, reishi and enokitake among the mushrooms grown at the farm.The business also expanded beyond selling fresh produce. Coffey explained that Mycoterra supplied mushroom-growing spawn to other cultivators and offered kits for people interested in growing mushrooms at home. She had also developed Mycoglow, a mushroom-based skincare range featuring products such as soaps, lotions, toners, bug sprays and scrubs.Fungi Academy describes mushroom cultivation as an activity that can serve several purposes, from supplying food to supporting small businesses. It highlights the potential for home growers to produce gourmet varieties, including oyster mushrooms, shiitake and lion's mane, without requiring conventional agricultural land.For Coffey, the operation also involved maintaining the quality of the mushrooms as production increased. Boston Voyager reported that Mycoterra maintained its own culture library and produced spawn in-house, rather than relying entirely on commercial suppliers.Boston Voyager reported that she identified short shelf life, a lack of familiarity with mushrooms among some consumers and the need to maintain sterile conditions during early growth as particular challenges.Coffey told Boston Voyager that she had regularly worked more than 60 hours a week for 8 years. Mushroom cultivation required continuous attention, leaving limited opportunities for time off. The new South Deerfield facility also created opportunities to reach wholesale markets while retaining sales through farmers markets and restaurants.
Article Summary: Julia Coffey began growing mushrooms in her basement in January 2010. She reinvested earnings into the operation, eventually moving beyond her basement to greenhouses and, later, a dedicated farming facility. Coffey's experience illustrated how a small operation could become more demanding as production increased.

Article Title: On Montana’s State Route 200, crews applied 3,000 gallons of magnesium chloride during and after a storm; the treated Plains section was bare afterwards and had a 37% lower four-year average cost per
Article Text:
A bare road on one side, packed snow on the other: The difference that early treatment can make (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

Two roads, one storm

Bare pavement after a storm: A key goal of winter road maintenance.(representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

What the cost figures showed

Acting early made the difference

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The limits of chemicals

Picture two stretches of the same highway after a winter storm. One is clear and dry, while the other is covered with packed snow and ice. According to the Federal Highway Administration case study, ‘ Montana DOT Anti-Icing/Deicing Operations ,’ a winter storm threatened State Route 200 in Montana on 14 December 2000. In the Plains section, crews applied 3,000 gallons (about 11,355 litres) of magnesium chloride during and after the storm. The result was a bare pavement.Two teams looked after the route. The Missoula maintenance division was responsible for Plains, while the Kalispell division was responsible for Thompson Falls. Both areas experienced different weather conditions. Plains received just 8 inches (20 cm) of snow. Thompson Falls, on the other hand, received 15 inches (38 cm) of snow followed by eight hours of freezing rain. Both places were about the same temperature.The two crews also chose different techniques. At Thompson Falls, 800 gallons of chemicals were used to pre-wet abrasives, which were then spread on the packed snow. An additional 750 gallons of magnesium chloride was used for anti-icing and de-icing in an area that didn't meet air quality standards.After the storm had passed, the road was covered by compacted snow and ice. Drivers complained about the sharp change where the two sections met.To understand the difference, the Montana Department of Transportation’s Maintenance Review Section interviewed managers and reviewed material used and operating costs from 1997 to 2000. These figures cover those four years, not the single storm. Plains had a four-year average of $1,095 per lane-mile annually. Thompson Falls had a four-year average of $1,750. A lane-mile is one mile of a single lane. That made Plains’ approach 37% cheaper. The savings were found in a variety of places. Labour cost 52% less. The cost of equipment was 44% lower. Sand was 44% cheaper, and crews used 41% less of it. Plains did spend more on magnesium chloride, $233 per lane-mile compared with $136. But it had a lower overall bill. The case study noted that Plains achieved a higher level of service with safety and mobility benefits, and fewer abrasives benefited the environment. Thompson Falls did face the heavier storm that day, but the cost averages span four winters.The review cited timing as a crucial factor here. Treatment with anti-icing products before or just as the storm started kept snow from compacting or made it easier to clear off. A later reaction required several rounds of material. It also offered only a temporary grip on snow-covered roads. This was the review’s general finding on preventive versus reactive treatment; the case study says only that Plains’ 3,000 gallons went on during and after the storm.Management practices were equally important. Plains managers ordered chemicals on the basis of an average winter and allowed the field supervisors to order additional amounts. By contrast, the managers of Kalispell estimated the requirement at the beginning of winter and bought no extra amount. Thus, Plains had a salt content of 7.5% in the sand mix, while Thompson Falls had 4%. Following the review, Kalispell raised its salt share from 4 to 7%.Magnesium chloride is not a cure-all for freezes. Researchers at Montana State University, writing in a 2025 report for the Montana Department of Transportation, put its working limit at -12°C, against about -9.4°C for common salt. They add that salt can accelerate the corrosion of steel in concrete bridges. The same report looks back at the Plains case. The researchers explain that the results show the cost-effectiveness of preventive treatment over reactive treatment. In their own work, they examine geothermal heat for bridge decks, tapping warmth from the ground. Lab tests and simulations suggested the system kept a bridge surface above freezing at -10°C with 10°C fluids entering the pipes. It's a feasibility study, so it does not prove the idea works on real bridges yet.
Article Summary: Winter storm threatened State Route 200 in Montana on 14 December 2000. Crews applied 3,000 gallons (about 11,355 litres) of magnesium chloride during and after the storm. Plains received just 8 inches (20 cm) of snow. Thompson Falls, on the other hand, received 15 inches of snow followed by eight hours of freezing rain.

Article Title: Families across 43 US states were offered rent-to-own plans advertised as 90-day deals but allegedly faced costs near twice the cash price; a proposed $183.5 million settlement would provide refunds a
Article Text:
How the 90-day offers allegedly turned into year-long payments

A $183.5 million settlement to help consumers

Company must change advertising and payment practices

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Families across 43 US states could receive refunds and debt relief under a proposed $183.5 million settlement with rent-to-own finance company Acima Digital, following allegations that the company misled customers about payment plans advertised as 90-day deals. According to Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday's November 12 announcement, the multistate agreement resolves allegations that consumers were automatically enrolled in rental-purchase agreements lasting up to 12 months, potentially leaving them paying nearly twice the original cash price of furniture, electronics and other merchandise. The settlement includes $43 million in consumer refunds, $130 million in lease balance reductions and $10.5 million for participating states.The agreement involves Acima Digital LLC and its parent company, Acima Holdings LLC. The company partners with retailers to offer customers rent-to-own arrangements, allowing them to obtain merchandise immediately and make payments over an agreed period. Such arrangements are often marketed as an alternative for people who may struggle to qualify for traditional credit or financing.However, attorneys general from 43 states alleged that Acima's advertising and enrolment practices gave customers an incomplete picture of what they were signing up for.The company allegedly promoted its rental-purchase agreements as 90-day payoff programmes without clearly explaining that customers could be automatically placed into agreements with a maximum term of 12 months.According to the allegations outlined by Pennsylvania and Ohio attorneys general, customers were attracted by advertisements suggesting they could pay off their merchandise within 90 days. However, the states claimed that Acima did not adequately disclose that consumers were automatically enrolled in longer rental-purchase agreements. Under these arrangements, customers could end up paying approximately twice the cash price advertised by the retailer if they continued with the full 12-month payment schedule.The states also alleged that Acima used terms such as "credit" in marketing its products, leading some consumers to believe they were signing up for conventional financing rather than a rental-purchase agreement. The distinction is significant because rent-to-own arrangements operate differently from traditional loans, with customers generally making payments to rent merchandise and having the option to acquire ownership under the agreement's terms.The investigation also raised concerns about how customers were presented with contracts. Attorneys general alleged that the company's electronic signing process obscured important terms and conditions, making it difficult for consumers to understand the full cost and duration of their agreements before accepting them.Another allegation concerned the process of ending these arrangements. The states claimed that Acima made it difficult for customers to terminate their agreements by returning merchandise, potentially leaving them with financial obligations they had expected to avoid. The coalition further alleged that the company marked up the cash prices of merchandise above the prices charged by its retail partners, adding to the amount consumers could ultimately pay.The proposed agreement divides the financial relief into three major components. According to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office, $43 million will be distributed as consumer restitution, $130 million will go towards reducing outstanding lease balances and $10.5 million will be paid to participating states.The Ohio Attorney General's Office provided a breakdown of the expected relief for residents in that state. Ohio consumers are expected to receive nearly $5 million in lease forgiveness across more than 4,000 agreements, while over $900,000 in restitution will be distributed among more than 3,000 customers.Pennsylvania, meanwhile, expects more than $1.6 million in consumer restitution and approximately $3.6 million in lease forgiveness. The state's attorney general said almost 9,000 Pennsylvania consumers could benefit from the settlement through refunds, paid-off leases or forgiven balances.Eligible consumers will not need to submit an application immediately to be considered for relief. Those entitled to restitution will be contacted by the settlement administrator, while customers eligible for lease forgiveness will be contacted directly by Acima. Further instructions will be provided to affected consumers.Beyond financial compensation, the agreement requires Acima to make changes to how it advertises and administers its rental-purchase agreements. The company must ensure that important information about payment periods, costs and contract conditions is clearly disclosed in its advertisements. It must also make the terms of agreements more visible during electronic signing, rather than presenting customers with processes that could obscure important details.Acima will also be required to stop marking up the cash prices charged by its retail partners and cannot obstruct customers from ending agreements by returning merchandise. The settlement additionally requires the company to train its retail partners so they can explain the arrangements more accurately.Another significant condition concerns credit reporting. Acima has agreed not to report these rental-purchase agreements to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, the three major US credit reporting agencies, for five years. The company must also properly address issues involving delayed deliveries, damaged merchandise and repairs where required by the agreement or state law.The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau had previously raised concerns about Acima's business model. In an amended complaint filed in September 2024, the agency alleged that the company's virtual rent-to-own arrangements could cost consumers more than twice the original retail price and that its enrolment and contract practices harmed customers. Those earlier allegations provide additional regulatory context to the latest multistate action.Acima's parent company, Upbound Group, said in a November 12 statement that the agreement resolves a multistate investigation dating back to 2021. The company said the settlement does not include findings or admissions of wrongdoing and that the payment had already been reserved in its 2025 financial statements.The consent petition has been filed in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas in Pennsylvania and is awaiting judicial approval. Until the court approves it, the proposed settlement is not final.For families affected by the alleged practices, the agreement could mean more than refunds. It could also eliminate outstanding lease balances and introduce changes intended to make the true cost of rent-to-own arrangements clearer before customers commit to them.
Article Summary: $183.5 million settlement with rent-to-own finance company Acima Digital. Allegations that the company misled customers about payment plans advertised as 90-day deals. $43 million in consumer refunds, $130 million in lease balance reductions and $10.5m for participating states.

Article Title: Jensen Huang's resignation, Chinese cyberattack and rogue AI: The conspiracy theories surrounding Microsoft outage
Article Text:
Microsoft Down: Outlook, Teams and Copilot Face Extended Global Outage

Jensen Huang's exit and Microsoft outage: Why are users connecting the two?

China attack theory: Is Beijing behind the outage?

Rogue AI theory: Did an AI agent cause the disruption?

What is Microsoft saying about the outage?

Laura Loomer questions Microsoft's government contracts

How widespread was the Microsoft outage?

NEW DELHI: A global Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and several other services has triggered a wave of conspiracy theories online, with social media users linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure, alleging a possible Chinese cyberattack and even speculating about a rogue AI agent.The outage, which began late Thursday (November 12) and continued into Friday, affected Microsoft's email, workplace communication and cloud-based services, leaving users across several countries struggling to access essential applications. While Microsoft attributed the disruption to infrastructure and server capacity problems, speculation about a possible cyberattack and other causes gained traction on social media.One theory linked the outage to Huang's departure from Nvidia, suggesting that the timing of the two developments was more than a coincidence. Another claimed that China could be behind an attack on US communications infrastructure, while some users questioned whether an artificial intelligence agent had gone rogue.However, Microsoft has said there is no indication that the disruption was caused by malicious activity or a cyberattack.The timing of the Microsoft disruption and the developments surrounding Huang's departure from Nvidia became a talking point on X.A user named Reese posted: "Jensen Huang stepped down and immediately after there is a global Microsoft outage. #noticing"The post suggested a connection between the two developments but offered no evidence to support the claim.The speculation comes amid a controversy surrounding Huang's departure from Nvidia, which has also drawn attention to the company's business relationships, national security concerns and the US technology sector.However, there is no evidence linking Huang's departure to Microsoft's technical problems.Another conspiracy theory circulating online suggested that the outage could be part of a Chinese cyber operation targeting US communications infrastructure.US political commentator Valentina Gomez claimed that the simultaneous developments involving Huang and Microsoft were not a coincidence.In a post on X, she wrote:"🚨Jensen Huang & Microsoft going DOWN on the same day is not a coincidence-911 systems are currently down-Credit cards/banking will go offline-If nuclear plants go offline for too long, it WILL be a huge problem.I think this is China attacking US communications grid"The post also raised concerns about the possible impact of a prolonged outage on emergency services, banking and critical infrastructure.However, no evidence has emerged to support the claim that China was responsible for the disruption. Microsoft has explicitly said its investigation has found no indication of malicious or cyber activity.Another theory circulating online suggested that an artificial intelligence system or autonomous AI agent could have triggered the disruption.The speculation gained attention as Microsoft's Copilot and other AI-related services were among the affected products.However, the company has not reported any evidence of an AI agent causing the outage. Microsoft has instead pointed to server availability, infrastructure load and an overwhelmed core process as the reasons behind the disruption.Charles Lamanna, executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents and Platform at Microsoft, addressed the speculation in a post on X."We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity".Microsoft initially said it was investigating reports of users facing difficulties accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods.Its subsequent investigation found that several servers had unexpectedly become unavailable after failing automated health checks. This reduced the available server capacity and pushed additional traffic onto the remaining infrastructure, resulting in connectivity problems.The company clarified that the elevated load was not caused by an overall increase in user traffic but by the reduced availability of servers.Microsoft also identified an overwhelmed core process on affected servers as a factor behind the capacity loss.The company said it was attempting to restore services by bringing affected servers back online, redistributing network traffic and exploring alternative recovery measures.However, its initial attempts to restore normal operations did not deliver the expected results.In an update on Friday, Microsoft 365 Status said: "We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected. We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as https://msft.it/6013xBHsf if the admin center is not available to you."Microsoft said it was continuing to work on restoring the affected services.The outage also triggered criticism of Microsoft's role in providing technology infrastructure to US government agencies.Political commentator Laura Loomer questioned the dependence of federal departments on Microsoft's cloud services and called for a review of the company's government contracts.In a post on X, she wrote: "Pretty crazy that Microsoft has been down all day. Our entire federal government runs on Microsoft Government Azure. Including the Department of War. This is a major national security threat and I’ve been saying for years now that @Microsoft needs to have all of their government contracts canceled. How many chances is Microsoft going to get? With all of those best and brightest H1B workers at Microsoft, I’m shocked they haven’t fixed the outage yet. 😏 I was told they are truly the best."Her remarks added to the debate over the risks of government agencies relying heavily on a single technology provider.The disruption affected several Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint Online and OneDrive.According to Downdetector, nearly 130,000 users worldwide reported problems at the peak of the outage.Users reported difficulties accessing email accounts, sending and receiving messages, loading inboxes and joining workplace meetings.The disruption also affected government departments and other organisations in different countries.Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade issued a notice directing urgent sanctions-related enquiries to the Australian Sanctions Office by telephone.The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry also warned that clients might be unable to send or receive emails through its systems.While the outage prompted concerns about the vulnerability of digital infrastructure and the dependence of organisations on cloud-based services, the conspiracy theories circulating online remain unsubstantiated.Microsoft's investigation, so far, points to technical and infrastructure-related problems rather than a confirmed cyberattack.
Article Summary: Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and several other services has triggered a wave of conspiracy theories online. Social media users linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure, alleging a possible Chinese cyberattack and even speculating about a rogue AI agent. Microsoft has said there is no indication that the disruption was caused by malicious activity or a cyberattack.

Article Title: A U.S. paratrooper and his London sweetheart lost touch after D-Day; more than 70 years later, he flew from Virginia to Australia to see her again
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing an elderly couple reuniting in an airport terminal. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A chance meeting in London before

D-Day

A misunderstanding that kept them apart for decades

U.S. paratroopers aboard a military aircraft during World War II, similar to the troops who traveled to England ahead of the D-Day invasion in June 1944. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A 10,000-mile journey for a long-awaited reunion

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A brief romance during the Second World War came to an end when a soldier was sent overseas. Decades later, a chance encounter and a missed taxi went in their favour as they discovered a wartime romance after more than 70 years apart. As reported by ABC News, the 93-year-old US Army veteran travelled to South Australia from his home in Virginia in February 2016 to reunite with his long-lost sweetheart, Joyce Durrant Morris.The pair met in London in 1944, when Joyce was 17 and Norwood Thomas was 21, during World War II . Their association had been cut short when he was deployed to the war front and rekindled by a series of letters, after which they lost touch. Until one of them did an internet search for their names over 70 years later. Donations and one airline helped the 93-year-old veteran make the extraordinary tripThomas and Morris first met in London in 1944, while American troops were in Britain preparing to go to war in Nazi-occupied Europe. Thomas was a member of the US Army 101st Airborne Division, an elite paratrooper unit that would arrive in France and take part in the Normandy landing on 6th June 1944. Their meeting was quite an accident. Another serviceman in his unit had stopped at a bridge spanning the River Thames when two young women appeared. The soldiers approached them, and Thomas and Morris eventually hit it off. They spent a few months together before he was posted away.The relationship came with obvious complications. During his service, Thomas was ultimately deployed to Normandy, where Americans parachuted behind enemy lines to support the Allied invasion. He sometimes tried to make his way back to London so that he could see Morris, even if just for a few days.
